overview: This record begins before Tanzania existed as a union. Tanganyika became independent in 1961; its 1964 union with Zanzibar created a state with both union and Zanzibar institutions. Later history includes socialist development projects, difficult rural reforms, international railway building and continuing community efforts in education.

sections.title: Institutions and an original Swahili title

items.text: The 1964 union brought Tanganyika and Zanzibar together, while retaining a separate Zanzibar government alongside the union government. The country’s political structure therefore cannot be understood simply as the mainland absorbing an island with no institutions of its own.

“Azimio la Arusha” means “Arusha Declaration”. The words appear in the title of TANU’s Swahili pamphlet of 1967, preserved in Indiana University’s collection. The short title introduces a document that shaped political debate about the country’s future.

The declaration outlined socialist policies associated with Julius Nyerere, including nationalization and restrictions on leaders’ private economic interests. Scholarship also traces debate among trade unionists and others: political ideas developed through argument as well as presidential speeches.

Later villagization included forcing rural people to move into planned villages. Promises of improved services did not remove the disruption of relocation or make every household willing to participate. Development history includes the choices governments denied people as well as the facilities they hoped to build.

The TAZARA railway linked Dar es Salaam with Kapiri Mposhi in Zambia. Tanzania, Zambia and China signed the construction agreement in 1967; full operations began on 14 July 1976. It provided a route to the coast outside the southern transport corridor controlled by white minority regimes.

The difficult Mlimba to Makambako section required bridges, tunnels and extensive earthworks. Chinese, Tanzanian and Zambian workers built the line together. A railway achievement includes surveying, construction and maintenance skills, rather than merely the moment a locomotive arrives.

Tanzania’s community-based adult education programme began in 1993. UNESCO describes learners meeting in primary schools after children went home, using Kiswahili and discussing practical topics such as farming, health and household finances. A classroom could have a second working day.

One group of women learned tailoring from a local craftsperson and used a group loan to buy a sewing machine for making school uniforms. Bookkeeping accompanied sewing skills. Reading and arithmetic helped connect lessons with running a small shared enterprise.

sections.title: Privacy at school and stories across borders

items.text: At Bahati School in Dar es Salaam, UNICEF’s 2017 report describes separate toilet blocks, handwashing stations, safe drinking water and an accessible toilet. The facilities made drinking, washing and taking a private break possible within the school day.

Students at Bahati took turns checking cleanliness, and a health teacher met girls to discuss puberty and hygiene. The menstrual hygiene room held clean pads. Privacy and an adult who will answer questions are practical parts of making a school usable.

Abdulrazak Gurnah, who grew up in Zanzibar, received the 2021 Nobel Prize in Literature. His novels explore colonialism and the experience of refugees across cultures. A literary achievement can carry a place’s difficult histories to readers far beyond its borders.

Gurnah left Zanzibar amid persecution in the 1960s and later settled in England. His life connects East Africa with a wider diaspora. His novels follow individuals crossing cultures and carrying memories of places they have left.

ending.text: Tanzania continues as the union formed in 1964. Independence, union and later reforms changed political institutions without ending the histories of mainland and island communities. The map’s 1960 start predates both Tanganyika’s independence and the union.
